prompt:
*(Power Round, Problem 1.1)* A **field** $F$ is a set with at least two elements and two binary operations $+$ and $\cdot$ satisfying: associativity of $+$ and $\cdot$; commutativity of $+$ and $\cdot$; existence of identities $0,1$ with $0+a=a$ and $1\cdot a=a$; additive inverses ($a+b=0$ for some $b$, written $-a$); multiplicative inverses for $a\ne0$ ($a\cdot b=1$ for some $b$, written $a^{-1}$); and distributivity $a(b+c)=ab+ac$.

Let $F$ be a field.

(a) (1 point) Prove that the additive identity and the multiplicative identity of $F$ are each unique.

(b) (1 point) Prove that every $a\in F$ has a unique additive inverse, and every nonzero $b\in F$ has a unique multiplicative inverse.

(c) (2 points) Prove that $0$ has no multiplicative inverse.
answer: Proofs of uniqueness of identities and inverses; $0\cdot b=0$ for all $b$ (distributivity) so $0$ has no inverse because $1\ne0$.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
**(a)** If $0$ and $0'$ are both additive identities, then $0'=0+0'$ (since $0$ is an identity) $=0'+0=0$ (since $0'$ is an identity, using commutativity). The same argument with $1,1'$ and multiplication gives $1=1'$.

**(b)** Suppose $b,b'$ are both additive inverses of $a$. Then
$$b=b+0=b+(a+b')=(b+a)+b'=0+b'=b'.$$
For a nonzero $c$ with multiplicative inverses $d,d'$: $d=d\cdot1=d(cd')=(dc)d'=1\cdot d'=d'$.

**(c)** First, $0\cdot x=0$ for every $x$: $0\cdot x=(0+0)x=0\cdot x+0\cdot x$; adding $-(0\cdot x)$ to both sides gives $0=0\cdot x$. If $0$ had an inverse $b$ then $1=0\cdot b=0$. Then for every $a\in F$, $a=1\cdot a=0\cdot a=0$, so $F=\{0\}$, contradicting that a field has at least two elements. The property used is distributivity (together with $|F|\ge2$, i.e. $1\ne0$). ∎

prompt:
*(Power Round, Problem 1.2)* A **vector space** $V$ over a field $F$ is a set with addition $V\times V\to V$ and scalar multiplication $F\times V\to V$ such that: $+$ is associative and commutative; there is a zero vector $0$ with $0+v=v$; every $v$ has an additive inverse $-v$; $1\cdot v=v$; $(ab)v=a(bv)$; and $a(v+w)=av+aw$, $(a+b)v=av+bv$.

Let $V$ be an $F$-vector space. A **subspace** of $V$ is a subset that is itself a vector space under the inherited operations. The **sum** of subspaces is $U+W=\{u+w: u\in U, w\in W\}$. If every element of $U_1+\cdots+U_n$ can be written *uniquely* as $\sum u_i$ with $u_i\in U_i$, the sum is called a **direct sum**, written $U_1\oplus\cdots\oplus U_n$. You may use $0v=0$, $a0=0$, $(-1)v=-v$.

(a) (1 point) Show that $W\subseteq V$ is a subspace if and only if $0\in W$ and $av+(-w)\in W$ for all $v,w\in W$, $a\in F$.

(b) (1 point) If $U,W$ are subspaces, prove that $U+W$ is a subspace of $V$.

(c) (2 points) Prove that $U_1+\cdots+U_n$ is the smallest subspace of $V$ containing every $U_i$ (any subspace containing all $U_i$ contains $U_1+\cdots+U_n$).

(d) (1 point) Prove that $U+W$ is a direct sum if and only if $U\cap W=\{0\}$.
answer: Subspace criterion; sums of subspaces are subspaces and are the smallest containing them; $U+W$ direct iff $U\cap W=\{0\}$.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
**(a)** ($\Rightarrow$) A subspace $W$ has its own zero vector $z$ with $z+z=z$; adding $-z$ gives $z=0$, so $0\in W$. By closure, $av\in W$ and $-w=(-1)w\in W$, hence $av+(-w)\in W$.

($\Leftarrow$) Take $a=1$, $v=0$: $-w\in W$ for all $w\in W$. Take $w=0$: $av\in W$ (closure under scalars). Then $v+w=1\cdot v+(-(-w))\in W$ (closure under addition). All axioms (associativity, commutativity, distributivity, $1v=v$, ...) hold in $W$ because they hold in $V$; the zero and inverses lie in $W$. So $W$ is a subspace.

**(b)** $0=0+0\in U+W$. If $u_1+w_1,\ u_2+w_2\in U+W$ and $a\in F$, then $a(u_1+w_1)-(u_2+w_2)=(au_1-u_2)+(aw_1-w_2)\in U+W$. By (a), $U+W$ is a subspace.

**(c)** By the argument of (b) (induction on $n$), $U_1+\cdots+U_n$ is a subspace. It contains each $U_i$ (take the other summands to be $0$). If $W'$ is any subspace containing every $U_i$, it is closed under addition, so it contains every sum $u_1+\cdots+u_n$ with $u_i\in U_i$, i.e. $U_1+\cdots+U_n\subseteq W'$.

**(d)** ($\Rightarrow$) If $x\in U\cap W$, then $x=x+0=0+x$ are two decompositions (first with $x\in U,0\in W$, then $0\in U$, $x\in W$); uniqueness forces $x=0$.
($\Leftarrow$) If $u_1+w_1=u_2+w_2$ then $u_1-u_2=w_2-w_1\in U\cap W=\{0\}$, so $u_1=u_2$ and $w_1=w_2$. ∎

prompt:
*(Power Round, Problem 1.3)* Let $F$ be a field. Define addition and scalar multiplication appropriately and prove the following.

(a) (1 point) The set of polynomials with coefficients in $F$ is a vector space over $F$, and for each $d\in\mathbb N$ the polynomials of degree at most $d$ form a subspace.

(b) (2 points) If $S$ is any set and $V$ is any $F$-vector space, then the set of all functions $S\to V$ is a vector space over $F$ (hint: define $(f+g)(s)=f(s)+g(s)$ and $(cf)(s)=cf(s)$).
answer: Check the vector space axioms coefficientwise / pointwise; use the subspace criterion for degree at most $d$.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
**(a)** Add polynomials and multiply by $c\in F$ coefficientwise: $\sum a_kx^k+\sum b_kx^k=\sum(a_k+b_k)x^k$, $c\sum a_kx^k=\sum(ca_k)x^k$. Each vector space axiom for a given coefficient is exactly the corresponding field axiom for $F$ (e.g. $(c+c')p$ has coefficients $(c+c')a_k=ca_k+c'a_k$). The zero polynomial is the zero vector and $-p$ has coefficients $-a_k$. So polynomials form a vector space.

For polynomials $p,q$ of degree at most $d$ and $a\in F$: the zero polynomial has degree at most $d$, and $ap-q$ has no terms above $x^d$. By Problem 1.2(a) the degree $\le d$ polynomials form a subspace.

**(b)** Let $\mathcal F$ be the set of functions $S\to V$ with $(f+g)(s)=f(s)+g(s)$ and $(cf)(s)=cf(s)$. Every axiom is checked pointwise using the same axiom in $V$. For example $((a+b)f)(s)=(a+b)f(s)=af(s)+bf(s)=(af+bf)(s)$, and $((f+g)+h)(s)=(f(s)+g(s))+h(s)=f(s)+(g(s)+h(s))=(f+(g+h))(s)$. The zero function $s\mapsto0$ is the zero vector, and $-f:s\mapsto-f(s)$ is the inverse of $f$. The remaining axioms are identical. ∎

prompt:
*(Power Round, Problem 1.4)* Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over a field $F$ (it is spanned by a finite set). A finite set $\{v_1,\dots,v_n\}$ is **linearly independent** if $a_1v_1+\cdots+a_nv_n=0$ implies all $a_i=0$, and is a **basis** if it is linearly independent and spans $V$.

**Lemma 1.7.** If $S=\{v_1,\dots,v_n\}$ is linearly dependent and spans $V$, then some $v_i\in\mathrm{span}(v_1,\dots,v_{i-1})$ and $S\setminus\{v_i\}$ still spans $V$. (You may cite the Lemma.)

(a) (2 points) **Theorem 1.8.** Any finite set that spans $V$ can be reduced (by removing elements) to a basis. In particular $V$ has a basis.

(b) (3 points) **Theorem 1.9.** Any spanning set of $V$ has at least as many elements as any linearly independent set in $V$.

(c) (2 points) **Theorem 1.10.** Any linearly independent set in $V$ can be extended to a basis.

Prove each theorem.
answer: Remove redundant vectors; exchange argument for $|\text{independent}|\le|\text{spanning}|$; extend by adding vectors outside the span.

solutions.title: Proofs
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $S$ span $V$. If $S$ is independent it is a basis. Otherwise by Lemma 1.7 we can delete one vector and still span. Repeat; each step reduces $|S|$, so the process stops, and it can only stop at a linearly independent spanning set, i.e. a basis. (If everything is removed we get $\emptyset$, which is a basis of $\{0\}$.)

**(b)** Let $w_1,\dots,w_m$ span $V$ and $u_1,\dots,u_k$ be independent. We show by induction on $j$ ($0\le j\le k$) that $j\le m$ and, after renumbering the $w$'s, $u_1,\dots,u_j,w_{j+1},\dots,w_m$ spans $V$. For $j=0$ this is given. Suppose it holds for $j<k$. Write
$$u_{j+1}=\sum_{i\le j}a_iu_i+\sum_{l>j}b_lw_l .$$
If all $b_l=0$ (including the case $j=m$, where there are no $w_l$ left), then $u_{j+1}-\sum a_iu_i=0$ is a nontrivial dependence, impossible. So $j<m$ and some $b_l\ne0$; renumber so $b_{j+1}\neq0$. Then
$$w_{j+1}=b_{j+1}^{-1}\Big(u_{j+1}-\sum_{i\le j}a_iu_i-\sum_{l>j+1}b_lw_l\Big),$$
so $w_{j+1}$ lies in the span of $u_1,\dots,u_{j+1},w_{j+2},\dots,w_m$, which therefore spans $V$, and $j+1\le m$. At $j=k$ we get $k\le m$.

**(c)** Let $L$ be independent. Any independent set has at most $m$ elements, where $m$ is the size of a fixed finite spanning set (part (b)), so among independent sets containing $L$ pick a maximal one $M$. Claim: $M$ spans $V$. If $v\notin\mathrm{span}(M)$, then $M\cup\{v\}$ is independent: from $av+\sum c_im_i=0$, if $a\ne0$ then $v=-a^{-1}\sum c_im_i\in\mathrm{span}(M)$, contradiction; so $a=0$ and then all $c_i=0$. This contradicts maximality. Hence $M$ is a basis containing $L$. ∎

prompt:
*(Power Round, Problem 1.5)* Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional vector space over $F$. The **dimension** $\dim V$ is the number of elements of any basis (all bases have the same size). Every linearly independent set extends to a basis. A sum $V_1+\cdots+V_n$ of subspaces is a **direct sum** $V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_n$ if every element has a unique expression $\sum v_i$ with $v_i\in V_i$; $U+W$ is direct iff $U\cap W=\{0\}$.

(a) (2 points) Suppose $V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_n$ is a direct sum of subspaces of $V$. Prove $\dim(V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_n)=\sum_i\dim V_i$ by concatenating bases of the $V_i$.

(b) (2 points) Prove that for any nontrivial proper subspace $U$ of $V$ there is a subspace $W$ with $U\oplus W=V$.
answer: Concatenated bases form a basis of a direct sum; extend a basis of $U$ to $V$ and let $W$ be the span of the added vectors.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $B_i$ be a basis of $V_i$ and let $B$ be the concatenation. $B$ spans $V_1+\cdots+V_n$ since every $v_i$ is a combination of $B_i$. For independence, suppose $\sum_i\sum_j a_{ij}b_{ij}=0$ where $B_i=\{b_{ij}\}$. Put $x_i=\sum_ja_{ij}b_{ij}\in V_i$; then $x_1+\cdots+x_n=0=0+\cdots+0$, so by uniqueness of the decomposition each $x_i=0$, and then independence of $B_i$ gives all $a_{ij}=0$. (In particular the $B_i$ are pairwise disjoint, since a common nonzero vector would lie in $V_i\cap V_j$, contradicting uniqueness.) Hence $B$ is a basis with $\sum|B_i|$ elements.

**(b)** Take a basis $u_1,\dots,u_k$ of $U$ and extend it to a basis $u_1,\dots,u_k,w_1,\dots,w_l$ of $V$ (Theorem 1.10). Let $W=\mathrm{span}(w_1,\dots,w_l)$. Every $v\in V$ is a combination of the basis, so $V=U+W$. If $x\in U\cap W$, write $x=\sum a_iu_i=\sum b_jw_j$; then $\sum a_iu_i-\sum b_jw_j=0$, so all coefficients vanish and $x=0$. Thus $U\cap W=\{0\}$ and the sum is direct. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.6)* Prove that $\mathbb R$ is a vector space over $\mathbb Q$. Is it infinite-dimensional or finite-dimensional? Justify your answer. If it is finite-dimensional, find the dimension. You may use that $\pi$ is transcendental (there is no nonzero polynomial $p$ with rational coefficients and $p(\pi)=0$), and that in a finite-dimensional vector space with a basis of $n$ elements, every set of $n+1$ vectors is linearly dependent.
answer: $\mathbb R$ is infinite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q$: $1,\pi,\pi^2,\dots$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$ by transcendence of $\pi$.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
**Vector space.** Take $V=\mathbb R$ with its usual addition and scalar multiplication by elements of $\mathbb Q\subset\mathbb R$. Every vector space axiom is a field axiom of $\mathbb R$ (associativity, commutativity, $0$ and $-x$, $1\cdot x=x$, distributivity), and $\mathbb Q\cdot\mathbb R\subseteq\mathbb R$ so scalar multiplication is well defined.

**Infinite-dimensional.** Suppose $\dim_{\mathbb Q}\mathbb R=n<\infty$. Consider $1,\pi,\pi^2,\dots,\pi^n$. If $a_0+a_1\pi+\cdots+a_n\pi^n=0$ with $a_k\in\mathbb Q$, then $p(x)=\sum a_kx^k$ is a rational polynomial with $p(\pi)=0$, so $p$ is the zero polynomial by transcendence and every $a_k=0$. Hence these $n+1$ numbers are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$ (in particular they are distinct), contradicting the fact that any $n+1$ vectors are dependent in an $n$-dimensional space. So $\mathbb R$ is infinite-dimensional over $\mathbb Q$. ∎

prompt:
*(Power Round, Problem 1.7)* A map $T:V\to W$ between vector spaces over $F$ is **linear** if $T(av)=aT(v)$ and $T(v+w)=T(v)+T(w)$ for all $a\in F$, $v,w\in V$. It is a **linear isomorphism** if it is linear, injective and surjective.

You may assume that the composition of two linear maps is linear.

(a) (1 point) Prove that if $T_1:U\to V$ and $T_2:V\to W$ are injective linear maps, then $T_2\circ T_1$ is an injective linear map.

(b) (1 point) Prove that if $T_1,T_2$ are surjective linear maps, then $T_2\circ T_1$ is a surjective linear map.

(c) (1 point) Let $T_1:U\to V$, $T_2:V\to W$ be linear maps with $T_2\circ T_1:U\to W$ a linear isomorphism. Prove that $T_1$ is injective and $T_2$ is surjective.
answer: Direct element-chasing with injectivity and surjectivity.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
**(a)** Linearity is given. If $T_2(T_1(x))=T_2(T_1(y))$ then $T_1(x)=T_1(y)$ since $T_2$ is injective, and then $x=y$ since $T_1$ is injective.

**(b)** Given $w\in W$, surjectivity of $T_2$ gives $v\in V$ with $T_2(v)=w$, and surjectivity of $T_1$ gives $u$ with $T_1(u)=v$. Then $(T_2\circ T_1)(u)=w$.

**(c)** If $T_1(x)=T_1(y)$ then $(T_2T_1)(x)=(T_2T_1)(y)$, so $x=y$ because $T_2T_1$ is injective; hence $T_1$ is injective. Given $w\in W$, surjectivity of $T_2T_1$ gives $u$ with $T_2(T_1(u))=w$, so $w=T_2(v)$ with $v=T_1(u)$; hence $T_2$ is surjective. ∎

prompt:
*(Power Round, Problem 1.8)* A map $T:V\to W$ between vector spaces over $F$ is **linear** if $T(av)=aT(v)$ and $T(v+w)=T(v)+T(w)$ for all $a\in F$, $v,w\in V$. It is a **linear isomorphism** if it is linear, injective and surjective.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear isomorphism of finite-dimensional vector spaces. Prove that $\dim V=\dim W$. (You may not cite the Rank-Nullity Theorem.)
answer: An isomorphism carries a basis of $V$ to a basis of $W$.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
Let $v_1,\dots,v_n$ be a basis of $V$. We claim $T(v_1),\dots,T(v_n)$ is a basis of $W$.

*Independent:* if $\sum a_iT(v_i)=0$ then $T(\sum a_iv_i)=0=T(0)$, so $\sum a_iv_i=0$ by injectivity (note $T(0)=T(0+0)=T(0)+T(0)$ gives $T(0)=0$), hence all $a_i=0$.

*Spanning:* for $w\in W$ pick $v=\sum a_iv_i$ with $T(v)=w$ (surjectivity); then $w=\sum a_iT(v_i)$.

So $\dim W=n=\dim V$. ∎

prompt:
*(Power Round, Problem 1.9)* A map $T:V\to W$ between vector spaces over $F$ is **linear** if $T(av)=aT(v)$ and $T(v+w)=T(v)+T(w)$ for all $a\in F$, $v,w\in V$. It is a **linear isomorphism** if it is linear, injective and surjective.

The **kernel** of $T$ is $\{v:T(v)=0\}$ and the **image** is $\{T(v):v\in V\}$. Consider $T:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^2$ given by $T((v_1,v_2,v_3))=(v_1,v_2)$. Prove that $T$ is linear, describe its kernel and image, and prove that the kernel has dimension $1$ and the image has dimension $2$ (explicitly verifying Rank-Nullity). Describe both vector spaces geometrically.
answer: Kernel is the $z$-axis $\{(0,0,t)\}$ (dim 1), image is all of $\mathbb R^2$ (dim 2); $1+2=3=\dim\mathbb R^3$.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
**Linear.** $T(a v)=(av_1,av_2)=aT(v)$ and $T(v+w)=(v_1+w_1,v_2+w_2)=T(v)+T(w)$.

**Kernel.** $T(v)=0$ iff $v_1=v_2=0$, so $\ker T=\{(0,0,t):t\in\mathbb R\}=\mathrm{span}\{(0,0,1)\}$. The single nonzero vector $(0,0,1)$ is independent and spans it, so $\dim\ker T=1$.

**Image.** For any $(a,b)\in\mathbb R^2$, $T((a,b,0))=(a,b)$, so the image is all of $\mathbb R^2$, which has the basis $(1,0),(0,1)$ and dimension $2$.

**Rank-Nullity.** $\dim\operatorname{im}T+\dim\ker T=2+1=3=\dim\mathbb R^3$.

**Geometry.** $\mathbb R^3$ is 3-dimensional space, $\mathbb R^2$ is the plane. $T$ projects each point straight down onto the $xy$-plane; the kernel is the $z$-axis (the line of points sent to the origin), and the image is the entire plane. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 1.10)* Let $A,B\in M_{m\times n}(F)$ be $m\times n$ matrices over a field $F$ (matrices act on column vectors $v\in F^n$ by matrix multiplication). Show that if $Av=Bv$ for all $v\in F^n$, then $A=B$.
answer: Apply to the standard basis vectors: $Ae_j$ is the $j$th column of $A$.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body: Let $e_j\in F^n$ be the standard basis vector with $1$ in position $j$ and $0$ elsewhere. For a matrix $A=(a_{ij})$, $(Ae_j)_i=\sum_ka_{ik}(e_j)_k=a_{ij}$, so $Ae_j$ is the $j$th column of $A$. Since $Ae_j=Be_j$ for every $j$, all columns of $A$ and $B$ agree, i.e. $a_{ij}=b_{ij}$ for all $i,j$. ∎

prompt:
*(Power Round, Problem 1.11)* Rotations of $\mathbb R^2$ are the linear maps
$$R_\theta\begin{pmatrix}a\\b\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\ \sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}a\\b\end{pmatrix}.$$
Composition of linear maps corresponds to multiplication of their matrices.

(a) (2 points) Prove that $R_{\theta_1}\circ R_{\theta_2}=R_{\theta_1+\theta_2}$ and $R_{-\theta}=R_\theta^{-1}$.

(b) (1 point) Verify that $R_\theta$ acts as a rotation by $\theta$ on the vector $\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}$ for any $\theta$.
answer: Matrix product plus angle-addition formulas; $R_\theta(1,0)=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
**(a)** Multiplying the matrices,
$$\begin{pmatrix}c_1&-s_1\\ s_1&c_1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}c_2&-s_2\\ s_2&c_2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}c_1c_2-s_1s_2&-(c_1s_2+s_1c_2)\\ s_1c_2+c_1s_2&c_1c_2-s_1s_2\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)&-\sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)\\ \sin(\theta_1+\theta_2)&\cos(\theta_1+\theta_2)\end{pmatrix}$$
by the angle-addition formulas, so $R_{\theta_1}\circ R_{\theta_2}=R_{\theta_1+\theta_2}$. Then $R_\theta\circ R_{-\theta}=R_0=I=R_{-\theta}\circ R_\theta$ (as $R_0$ has matrix $I$), so $R_{-\theta}=R_\theta^{-1}$.

**(b)** $R_\theta\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta\\ \sin\theta\end{pmatrix}$, the point on the unit circle at angle $\theta$ counterclockwise from $(1,0)$. This is $(1,0)$ rotated by $\theta$ about the origin. ∎

prompt:
*(Power Round, Problem 1.12)* Let $v_1,\dots,v_n$ and $w_1,\dots,w_n$ be two bases of $V$. If $v_i=a_{1i}w_1+\cdots+a_{ni}w_n$, the matrix $B=(a_{ij})$ is the **change of basis matrix** from the $v$-basis to the $w$-basis: it takes the coordinate vector of a vector in the $v$-basis to its coordinate vector in the $w$-basis. You may use $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}=(ad-bc)I$.

Find the change of basis matrix from $\{(1,0),(0,1)\}$ to $\{(2,3),(1,4)\}$ in $\mathbb R^2$. Then express $(6,5)$ as a linear combination of $(2,3)$ and $(1,4)$.

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
Let $M=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$, whose columns are the new basis vectors written in the standard basis; it converts coordinates from the new basis to the standard one. We need the opposite direction, so $B=M^{-1}$. The hint with $\det M=2\cdot4-1\cdot3=5$ gives
$$B=M^{-1}=\frac15\begin{pmatrix}4&-1\\-3&2\end{pmatrix}.$$
(Check: $(1,0)=\tfrac45(2,3)-\tfrac35(1,4)$, matching the first column; $(0,1)=-\tfrac15(2,3)+\tfrac25(1,4)$, matching the second.)

The coordinates of $(6,5)$ in the new basis are
$$B\begin{pmatrix}6\\5\end{pmatrix}=\frac15\begin{pmatrix}24-5\\-18+10\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}19/5\\-8/5\end{pmatrix}.$$
Check: $\tfrac{19}{5}(2,3)-\tfrac85(1,4)=\big(\tfrac{38-8}{5},\tfrac{57-32}{5}\big)=(6,5)$.

**Answer:** $B=\frac15\begin{pmatrix}4&-1\\-3&2\end{pmatrix}$ and $(6,5)=\frac{19}{5}(2,3)-\frac85(1,4)$. ∎

prompt:
*(Power Round, Problem 1.13)* A sum $V_1+\cdots+V_m$ of subspaces of $V$ is a **direct sum** $V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_m$ if every element has a unique expression $\sum v_i$ with $v_i\in V_i$.

Prove that if $V_1,\dots,V_m\subseteq V$ are subspaces and $U_i\subseteq V_i$ are subspaces, then $V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_m$ implies $U_1\oplus\cdots\oplus U_m$. (If the sum of the $V_i$ is direct, then the sum of the $U_i$ is direct.)
answer: Uniqueness in the larger sum implies uniqueness in the smaller sum.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body: Suppose $u_1+\cdots+u_m=u_1'+\cdots+u_m'$ with $u_i,u_i'\in U_i$. Since $U_i\subseteq V_i$, both sides are decompositions of the same vector in $V_1+\cdots+V_m$ with $i$th term in $V_i$. *(Power Round, Problem 1.15)* Let $F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ ($a^*$ denotes the complex conjugate). An **inner product** $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle$ on $V$ is additive in each argument, satisfies $\langle cv,w\rangle=c\langle v,w\rangle$, $\langle v,cw\rangle=c^*\langle v,w\rangle$, $\langle v,w\rangle=\langle w,v\rangle^*$, and $\langle v,v\rangle\ge0$ with equality iff $v=0$. (b) (1 point) If $v=a_1v_1+\cdots+a_nv_n$ in an orthonormal basis, prove $\langle v,v\rangle=a_1a_1^*+\cdots+a_na_n^*$.

(c) (4 points) Let $B$ be the change of basis matrix from an orthonormal basis $v_1,\dots,v_n$ to another orthonormal basis $w_1,\dots,w_n$ (so $v_i=\sum_kb_{ki}w_k$). Prove that the columns of $B$ are orthonormal vectors in $F^n$ and that the rows of $B$ are orthonormal vectors in $F^n$.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
**(a)** Write $v=\sum a_iv_i$. Then $\langle v,v_j\rangle=\sum_ia_i\langle v_i,v_j\rangle=a_j$. So $v=\sum_j\langle v,v_j\rangle v_j$.

**(b)** $\langle v,v\rangle=\sum_{i,j}a_ia_j^*\langle v_i,v_j\rangle=\sum_ia_ia_i^*$.

$$\delta_{ij}=\langle v_i,v_j\rangle=\sum_{k,l}b_{ki}b_{lj}^*\langle w_k,w_l\rangle=\sum_kb_{ki}b_{kj}^*=\langle\mathrm{col}_i(B),\mathrm{col}_j(B)\rangle,$$

solutions.title: Rule and proof
solutions.body:
**Rotations.** The inverse of the counterclockwise rotation by $\theta$ is the rotation by $\theta$ clockwise, i.e. $R_\theta^{-1}=R_{360^\circ-\theta}$: indeed $R_\theta\circ R_{360^\circ-\theta}=R_{360^\circ}=I$ and likewise in the other order. For the triangle $R_{120}^{-1}=R_{240}$; for the square $R_{90}^{-1}=R_{270}$ and $R_{180}^{-1}=R_{180}$.

**Flips.** Every flip is its own inverse: $F\circ F=I$. A flip is a reflection of the polygon in a line through the center; reflecting twice in the same line returns every point to its original place. (Equivalently, it is a half-turn about the line in space, and two half-turns give a full turn.) This matches the tables: the diagonal entries at the flips are $I$. ∎

(b) (1 point) Label the vertices of $P_n$ with the vertex labelled $2$ directly counterclockwise from the vertex labelled $1$. solutions.body:
**Description of $D_n$.** Number the vertices $0,1,\dots,n-1$ counterclockwise (vertex $k$ carries label $k+1$) and read positions mod $n$. So $D_n=\{T_{s,a}\}$ and $|D_n|=2n$. Moreover $T_{s,a}\circ T_{s',a'}=T_{ss',\,sa'+a}$ and $T_{s,a}$ is a rotation exactly when $s=1$.

**(a)** Done above: exactly the $2n$ maps $x\mapsto sx+a$.

**(b)** After applying $T$, the vertex labelled $1$ sits at position $T(0)=a$ and the vertex labelled $2$ at $T(1)=s+a$. Label $2$ is counterclockwise to $1$ iff $s=+1$, which happens for exactly the $n$ values of $a$. The other $n$ symmetries have $s=-1$: $2$ is clockwise to $1$. ∎

*(Power Round, Problem 2.11)* Let $P_n$ ($n\ge3$) be a regular $n$-gon in $\mathbb R^3$ with circumcenter at the origin. A **symmetry transformation** of $P_n$ is a bijective map of $P_n$ onto itself that is effected by a rotation of $\mathbb R^3$ about an axis through the origin. $D_n$ denotes the set of these transformations; the composition of two of them is again one. A symmetry that keeps the labelling "$2$ counterclockwise to $1$" (for vertices labelled $1,2,\dots,n$ counterclockwise) is called a rotation, otherwise a flip. $I$ is the identity. Compositions are written $T\circ S$ ($S$ first).

All transformations below lie in $D_n$.

(a) (1 point) Show that for two rotations $R,R'$ we have $R\circ R'=R'\circ R$.

(b) (1 point) Show that for a rotation $R$ and a flip $F$, $F\circ R\circ F=R^{-1}$. When is $R\circ F=F\circ R$?

(c) (1 point) For two flips $F,F'$, when is $F\circ F'=F'\circ F$? (Hint: use the previous part and Problem 2.10.)
answer: (a) rotations commute; (b) $FRF=R^{-1}$, and $RF=FR$ iff $R=I$ or $R$ is the half-turn ($n$ even); (c) iff $F=F'$ or ($n$ even and the mirror lines are perpendicular).

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
**Description of $D_n$.** Number the vertices $0,1,\dots,n-1$ counterclockwise (vertex $k$ carries label $k+1$) and read positions mod $n$. A rotation of $\mathbb R^3$ preserving $P_n$ maps vertices to vertices and adjacent vertices to adjacent vertices (it is an isometry), and a rotation is determined by the images of two linearly independent vectors (the third direction is determined by cross products). Vertices $0$ and $1$ are independent, so a symmetry $T$ is determined by $T(0)=a$ ($n$ choices) and $T(1)=a\pm1$ (two choices): at most $2n$ symmetries, and they act on vertices as $T_{s,a}(x)=sx+a \pmod n$ with $s=\pm1$, $a\in\mathbb Z_n$. Each of these occurs: $T_{1,a}$ is the rotation about the axis perpendicular to the plane of $P_n$ by $2\pi a/n$; $T_{-1,a}$ is the half-turn about the line through the origin in the plane of $P_n$ at angle $\pi a/n$ from vertex $0$ (a mirror line of $P_n$), which acts on the plane as the reflection $x\mapsto a-x$. So $D_n=\{T_{s,a}\}$ and $|D_n|=2n$. Moreover $T_{s,a}\circ T_{s',a'}=T_{ss',\,sa'+a}$ and $T_{s,a}$ is a rotation exactly when $s=1$.

**(a)** $T_{1,a}\circ T_{1,b}(x)=x+a+b=T_{1,b}\circ T_{1,a}(x)$.

**(b)** Let $F=T_{-1,c}$, $R=T_{1,b}$. Then $F(R(F(x)))=-(-x+c+b)+c=x-b=R^{-1}(x)$. Also $R\circ F(x)=-x+c+b$ and $F\circ R(x)=-x-b+c$; these agree iff $2b\equiv0\pmod n$, i.e. $R=I$ or $n$ is even and $R$ is the half-turn $b=n/2$.

**(c)** $F\circ F'$ is a rotation $R$ (sign $(-1)(-1)=1$), and $F'\circ F=(F\circ F')^{-1}=R^{-1}$ (since $(F F')^{-1}=F'^{-1}F^{-1}=F'F$). So $FF'=F'F$ iff $R=R^{-1}$ iff $R^2=I$ iff $R=I$ or $R$ is the half-turn. $R=I$ means $F=F'$. $R$ is a half-turn only when $n$ is even; writing $F=T_{-1,c}$, $F'=T_{-1,c'}$ we have $FF'(x)=x+c-c'$, so the condition is $c-c'=n/2$, i.e. the two mirror lines make an angle of $90^\circ$ (perpendicular). ∎

prompt:
*(Power Round, Problem 2.12)* Let $\mathbf n=\{1,\dots,n\}$. A **permutation** of $\mathbf n$ is a bijection $p:\mathbf n\to\mathbf n$; $S_n$ is the set of all of them, and $p^k$ is the $k$-fold composition $p\circ\cdots\circ p$.

(a) (1 point) Show that for $p,q\in S_n$, $p\circ q\in S_n$.

(b) (1 point) Show that for any $p\in S_n$ and $a\in\mathbf n$ there is $k\ge1$ with $p^k(a)=a$.
answer: Composition of bijections is a bijection; pigeonhole on $a,p(a),p^2(a),\dots$

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
**(a)** If $p(q(x))=p(q(y))$ then $q(x)=q(y)$ ($p$ injective) so $x=y$ ($q$ injective). Given $z$, pick $y$ with $p(y)=z$ and $x$ with $q(x)=y$; then $p(q(x))=z$. So $p\circ q$ is a bijection.

**(b)** The $n+1$ values $a,p(a),\dots,p^n(a)$ lie in an $n$-element set, so $p^i(a)=p^j(a)$ for some $0\le i<j\le n$. Applying the injective map $p^{-i}$ (i times the inverse) gives $a=p^{j-i}(a)$ with $k=j-i\ge1$. ∎

*(Power Round, Problem 2.13)* For $p\in S_n$ and $a\in\mathbf n$ the **orbit** of $a$ is $\mathrm{Orb}_p(a)=\{p^m(a):m\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\}$ (with $p^0=\mathrm{id}$). You may use that for every $a$ there is $k\ge1$ with $p^k(a)=a$.

(a) (1 point) Show that for all $b\in\mathrm{Orb}_p(a)$, $\mathrm{Orb}_p(b)=\mathrm{Orb}_p(a)$.

(b) (2 points) Show that $\mathbf n$ can be broken into disjoint sets $A_1\cup\cdots\cup A_k$ such that $a,b$ are in the same set iff $b\in\mathrm{Orb}_p(a)$.
answer: The relation $b\in\mathrm{Orb}_p(a)$ is an equivalence relation; its classes are the orbits.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $b=p^m(a)$. Then $p^t(b)=p^{t+m}(a)\in\mathrm{Orb}_p(a)$, so $\mathrm{Orb}_p(b)\subseteq\mathrm{Orb}_p(a)$. Conversely let $p^k(a)=a$, $k\ge1$ and choose $t$ with $kt\ge m$. Then $p^{kt-m}(b)=p^{kt}(a)=a$, so $a\in\mathrm{Orb}_p(b)$, and then every $p^u(a)=p^{u+kt-m}(b)\in\mathrm{Orb}_p(b)$. Hence the orbits are equal.

**(b)** Define $a\sim b$ iff $b\in\mathrm{Orb}_p(a)$. Reflexive: $a=p^0(a)$. Symmetric: if $b\in\mathrm{Orb}_p(a)$ then $\mathrm{Orb}_p(b)=\mathrm{Orb}_p(a)\ni a$ by (a). Transitive: if $b\in\mathrm{Orb}_p(a)$ and $c\in\mathrm{Orb}_p(b)=\mathrm{Orb}_p(a)$ then $a\sim c$. So $\sim$ is an equivalence relation, and its classes $A_1,\dots,A_k$ are disjoint with union $\mathbf n$; the class of $a$ is exactly $\mathrm{Orb}_p(a)$. ∎

(a) (1 point) $(1\ 3\ 4)(2\ 3\ 1)$

(b) (1 point) $(1\ 2\ 4)(4\ 5\ 3)(5\ 4\ 3)(4\ 2\ 1)$

(c) (1 point) $\tau\circ\sigma$, where $\sigma=(6\ 1\ 3)(4\ 2)$ and $\tau=(1\ 2\ 5\ 6\ 3\ 7)$.

solutions.title: Computation
solutions.body:
**(a)** $(2\,3\,1)$ sends $1\to2,\ 2\to3,\ 3\to1$; then $(1\,3\,4)$ sends $1\to3,\ 3\to4,\ 4\to1$. Composite: $1\to2\to2$; $2\to3\to4$; $4\to4\to1$; $3\to1\to3$. So the result is $(1\ 2\ 4)$.

**(b)** $(4\,5\,3)(5\,4\,3)$ is a cycle times its inverse, so it is the identity; likewise $(1\,2\,4)(4\,2\,1)$ ($(4\,2\,1)=(1\,4\,2)=(1\,2\,4)^{-1}$) is the identity. The whole product is the **identity**.

**(c)** $\sigma$: $6\to1\to3\to6$, $4\leftrightarrow2$. $\tau$: $1\to2\to5\to6\to3\to7\to1$. Composite: $1\to3\to7$, $7\to7\to1$; $2\to4\to4$, $4\to2\to5$, $5\to5\to6$, $6\to1\to2$; $3\to6\to3$. So $\tau\circ\sigma=(1\ 7)(2\ 4\ 5\ 6)$.

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.15)* A permutation $p\in S_n$ has a cycle decomposition $C_1C_2\cdots C_k$ into disjoint cycles, where $(a_1\ a_2\ \cdots\ a_m)$ sends $a_i\mapsto a_{i+1}$ and $a_m\mapsto a_1$. Given a cycle decomposition of $p$, describe the cycle decomposition of its inverse $q$ (the permutation with $p\circ q=q\circ p=I$), and prove your answer.
answer: Reverse each cycle: $(a_1\ a_2\ \cdots\ a_m)^{-1}=(a_m\ \cdots\ a_2\ a_1)$.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
Claim: if $p=C_1\cdots C_k$ with $C_i=(a^{(i)}_1\ \cdots\ a^{(i)}_{m_i})$, then $p^{-1}=C_1'\cdots C_k'$ where $C_i'=(a^{(i)}_{m_i}\ \cdots\ a^{(i)}_1)$ is the cycle written backwards, with the same disjoint supports.

Take $x$ in the support of $C_i$, say $x=a_j$ (indices mod $m_i$). Then $p(x)=a_{j+1}$ since the other cycles fix it. The permutation $q$ defined by the reversed cycles sends $a_{j+1}\mapsto a_j$, so $q(p(a_j))=a_j$. Elements outside all cycles are fixed by both. Hence $q\circ p=I$, and $p\circ q=I$ similarly, so $q=p^{-1}$. ∎

*(Power Round, Problem 2.16)* Let $n\ge2$. Every permutation in $S_n$ is a product of transpositions, and the parity of the number of transpositions is determined by the permutation (even/odd permutation). Products of two even permutations and inverses of even permutations are even. Let $A_n$ be the set of even permutations and $B_n=S_n\setminus A_n$ the odd ones.

(a) (1 point) Show that $A_n$ and $B_n$ have the same size, and that for any fixed $\sigma\in B_n$, $B_n=\{\sigma\circ\tau:\tau\in A_n\}$.

(b) (1 point) Show that if $\tau_i\in A_n$ and $\sigma_i\in B_n$, then $\tau_1\circ\tau_2\in A_n$, $\tau_1\circ\sigma_1\in B_n$, $\sigma_1\circ\tau_1\in B_n$ and $\sigma_1\circ\sigma_2\in A_n$.
answer: Left multiplication by an odd $\sigma$ is a bijection $A_n\to B_n$; parities add.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
Writing an even/odd permutation as a product of $k$ transpositions, the number of transpositions in a product is the sum of the counts, so parities add: even$\cdot$even=even, even$\cdot$odd=odd, odd$\cdot$odd=even. This proves **(b)**.

**(a)** Fix odd $\sigma$. The map $\tau\mapsto\sigma\circ\tau$ sends $A_n$ into $B_n$ by (b). It is injective ($\sigma\tau=\sigma\tau'\Rightarrow\tau=\tau'$ by applying $\sigma^{-1}$). It is onto $B_n$: for $\beta\in B_n$, $\sigma^{-1}$ is odd (reverse the product of transpositions of $\sigma$; same count), so $\tau=\sigma^{-1}\beta$ is even by (b), and $\beta=\sigma\tau$. So $B_n=\{\sigma\tau:\tau\in A_n\}$ and $|A_n|=|B_n|$. ∎

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
Label the vertices of $P_3$ by $1,2,3$. Every $T\in D_3$ maps vertices to vertices bijectively, so it induces a permutation $\phi(T)\in S_3$: $\phi(T)(i)=$ the label of the vertex to which $T$ sends vertex $i$.

*Homomorphism:* $\phi(a\circ b)(i)$ is the vertex $a(b(i))$, which is $\phi(a)(\phi(b)(i))$. So $\phi(a\circ b)=\phi(a)\circ\phi(b)$.

*Injective:* a symmetry is determined by the images of two vertices (shown in Problem 2.8), so if $\phi(T)=\phi(T')$ then $T=T'$.

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.18)* A (rigid) **symmetry transformation** of a cube $P$ with center at the origin is a bijective map of $P$ onto itself effected by a rotation of $\mathbb R^3$ about an axis through $0$. Let $G$ be the set of symmetry transformations of the cube, under composition. Show that there is a bijection $\phi:G\to S_4$ such that $\phi(a\circ b)=\phi(a)\circ\phi(b)$ for all $a,b\in G$.
answer: Let $G$ act on the four space diagonals of the cube; this gives an injective homomorphism $G\to S_4$ and $|G|=24=|S_4|$.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
Take the cube $[-1,1]^3$ with vertices $(\pm1,\pm1,\pm1)$. The four space diagonals are the lines $L_1,\dots,L_4$ through opposite vertices, spanned by $v_1=(1,1,1)$, $v_2=(1,1,-1)$, $v_3=(1,-1,1)$, $v_4=(-1,1,1)$.

**$|G|=24$.** A rotation $g$ preserving the cube maps vertices to vertices, edges to edges and faces to faces, hence the face centers $\pm e_1,\pm e_2,\pm e_3$ to face centers. So $g$ is a signed permutation matrix, and rotation means $\det g=1$. There are $3!\cdot2^3=48$ signed permutation matrices, and exactly half have determinant $+1$ (multiplying by $-I$ switches the sign). Conversely each such matrix is a rotation preserving the cube. Hence $|G|=24$.

**The homomorphism.** $g\in G$ maps diagonals to diagonals (opposite vertices to opposite vertices), so it permutes $L_1,\dots,L_4$: define $\phi(g)\in S_4$ by $g(L_i)=L_{\phi(g)(i)}$. Then $\phi(a\circ b)=\phi(a)\circ\phi(b)$, since $a(b(L_i))=a(L_{\phi(b)(i)})=L_{\phi(a)(\phi(b)(i))}$.

**Injective.** Suppose $\phi(g)=\mathrm{id}$. Then $g v_i=\varepsilon_iv_i$ with $\varepsilon_i=\pm1$ (it is an isometry, so it preserves lengths). Rotations preserve inner products, and $\langle v_1,v_j\rangle=1$ for $j=2,3,4$, so $\varepsilon_1\varepsilon_j=1$; all $\varepsilon_i$ are equal to a common $\varepsilon$. As $v_1,v_2,v_3$ form a basis, $g=\varepsilon I$. Since $\det g=1$ and $\det(-I)=-1$, $\varepsilon=1$ and $g=I$. So $\ker\phi$ is trivial and $\phi$ is injective.

**Bijective.** $\phi$ is injective from a 24-element set to $S_4$, which also has $24$ elements. So $\phi$ is a bijection. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 2.19)* A (rigid) **symmetry transformation** of a regular dodecahedron $P$ centered at the origin is a bijective map of $P$ onto itself effected by a rotation of $\mathbb R^3$ about an axis through $0$. Let $G$ be the group of these under composition. Show that there is a bijection $\phi:G\to A_5$ such that $\phi(a\circ b)=\phi(a)\circ\phi(b)$ for all $a,b\in G$. ($A_5$ is the group of even permutations of $\{1,\dots,5\}$.) Hint: consider the figure, which shows a cube inscribed in the dodecahedron.
answer: $G$ permutes the five cubes inscribed in the dodecahedron; $\phi:G\to S_5$ is injective, $|G|=60$, and the image of index 2 must be $A_5$.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
Put $\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}{2}$ and $a=1/\varphi=\varphi-1$. Take the dodecahedron with the 20 vertices $(\pm1,\pm1,\pm1)$, $(0,\pm a,\pm\varphi)$, $(\pm a,\pm\varphi,0)$, $(\pm\varphi,0,\pm a)$. The 8 vertices $(\pm1,\pm1,\pm1)$ form an inscribed cube $C_0$ (figure).

**Step 1: $|G|=60$.** The half-turn about the axis through the midpoint of an edge swaps the two faces sharing that edge; since any two of the 12 faces are linked by a chain of adjacent faces, $G$ is transitive on the 12 faces. A rotation preserving a face $F_0$ is a rotation about its axis through the center, by a multiple of $72^\circ$, giving 5 elements. A rotation is determined by the images of two independent vectors (the center of $F_0$ and a vertex $v_0$ of $F_0$), i.e. by the pair (face, vertex of that face): at most $12\cdot5=60$ choices, and all occur (move $F_0$ to any face, then rotate about the axis). So $|G|=60$.

**Step 2: five cubes.** Let $H=\{g\in G:g(C_0)=C_0\}$. $H$ consists of cube rotations (signed permutation matrices of determinant $1$) that preserve the vertex set $V$. The 12 matrices that cyclically permute the coordinates and change signs of an even number of coordinates preserve $V$ (cyclic shifts permute the three families $(0,\pm a,\pm\varphi)\to(\pm a,\pm\varphi,0)\to(\pm\varphi,0,\pm a)$ and sign changes preserve each family). The other 12 cube rotations involve swapping two coordinates; they send $(0,a,\varphi)$ to $(\pm a,0,\pm\varphi)$, $(\pm\varphi,\pm a,0)$ or $(0,\pm\varphi,\pm a)$, none of which is a vertex. So $|H|=12$. By the orbit-stabilizer count (the map $gH\mapsto g(C_0)$ is a bijection from left cosets of $H$ to the orbit), the orbit of $C_0$ under $G$ has $60/12=5$ cubes. Explicitly, rotating by $72^\circ$ about the face axis through $(0,\varphi,1)$ (a symmetry) gives the orbit $C_0,C_1,\dots,C_4$:
- $C_1$: $(-\varphi,0,a),(-1,1,-1),(-a,-\varphi,0),(0,-a,-\varphi),(0,a,\varphi),(a,\varphi,0),(1,-1,1),(\varphi,0,-a)$
- $C_2$: $(-\varphi,0,a),(-1,-1,-1),(-a,\varphi,0),(0,-a,\varphi),(0,a,-\varphi),(a,-\varphi,0),(1,1,1),(\varphi,0,-a)$
- $C_3$: $(-\varphi,0,-a),(-1,1,1),(-a,-\varphi,0),(0,-a,\varphi),(0,a,-\varphi),(a,\varphi,0),(1,-1,-1),(\varphi,0,a)$
- $C_4$: $(-\varphi,0,-a),(-1,-1,1),(-a,\varphi,0),(0,-a,-\varphi),(0,a,\varphi),(a,-\varphi,0),(1,1,-1),(\varphi,0,a)$.

Inspection shows: **any two of the five cubes share exactly two vertices, and these are antipodal** (e.g. $C_0\cap C_1=\{\pm(1,-1,1)\}$, $C_1\cap C_2=\{\pm(\varphi,0,-a)\}$, $C_3\cap C_4=\{\pm(\varphi,0,a)\}$, and so on for all 10 pairs). The ten pairs account for all $20=10\cdot2$ vertices.

**Step 3: the homomorphism.** $G$ permutes the five cubes; label them $1,\dots,5$ and define $\phi(g)\in S_5$ accordingly. As in Problem 2.18, $\phi(a\circ b)=\phi(a)\circ\phi(b)$.

**Step 4: injective.** If $\phi(g)=\mathrm{id}$, $g$ fixes every cube, hence maps each intersection $C_i\cap C_j=\{v,-v\}$ to itself. Every vertex lies in such an intersection, so $gv=\pm v$ for every vertex $v$. Applying this to $u_1=(1,1,1)$, $u_2=(1,1,-1)$, $u_3=(1,-1,1)$ (a basis, with $\langle u_1,u_2\rangle=\langle u_1,u_3\rangle=1$), $g$ preserves inner products so the signs agree, $g=\varepsilon I$, and $\det g=1$ forces $g=I$.

**Step 5: image is $A_5$.** $\phi(G)$ is a subgroup of $S_5$ of order $60$, so of index $2$. An index-2 subgroup $K$ is normal (its left and right cosets are both $K$ and the complement), and the quotient $S_5/K$ has order 2, so $g^2\in K$ for every $g\in S_5$. A 3-cycle $c$ satisfies $c=(c^2)^2\in K$. The 3-cycles generate $A_5$ (each even permutation is a product of pairs of transpositions, and $(a\ b)(b\ c)=(a\ b\ c)$, $(a\ b)(c\ d)=[(a\ b)(b\ c)][(b\ c)(c\ d)]$). So $A_5\subseteq K$, and as $|K|=60=|A_5|$, $K=A_5$.

Hence $\phi:G\to A_5$ is a bijective homomorphism. ∎

*(Power Round, Problem 2.20)* A **group** is a nonempty set $G$ with an identity $e\in G$ and a binary operation $\cdot:G\times G\to G$ such that: (associativity) $x(yz)=(xy)z$; (identity) $ex=xe=x$; (inverse) for each $x$ there is $y$ with $xy=yx=e$ (written $x^{-1}$). It is **abelian** if also $xy=yx$. A nonempty subset $H$ of $G$ is a **subgroup** ($H\le G$) if $xy\in H$ and $x^{-1}\in H$ for all $x,y\in H$. For $g\in G$, the **left coset** is $gH=\{gh:h\in H\}$ and the right coset is $Hg=\{hg:h\in H\}$.

Let $G$ be a group.

(a) (1 point) Show that inverses are unique: if $x\cdot y_1=x\cdot y_2=e$ then $y_1=y_2$.

(b) (1 point) Show that if $xy=xz$ then $y=z$; and if $zx=yx$ then $y=z$.

(c) (1 point) Show that $f_x:G\to G$, $f_x(y)=xy$ and $g_x:G\to G$, $g_x(y)=yx$ are bijections.
answer: Use the two-sided inverse $x^{-1}$ and associativity; cancellation gives injectivity, and $y=f_x(x^{-1}y)$ gives surjectivity.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
**(a)** Let $x'$ be an element with $x'x=xx'=e$ (it exists by the inverse axiom). If $xy_1=e$ then $y_1=ey_1=(x'x)y_1=x'(xy_1)=x'e=x'$. The same computation for $y_2$ gives $y_2=x'$. So $y_1=y_2$.

**(b)** From $xy=xz$ multiply on the left by $x^{-1}$: $y=(x^{-1}x)y=x^{-1}(xy)=x^{-1}(xz)=z$. From $zx=yx$ multiply on the right by $x^{-1}$: $z=y$.

**(c)** $f_x$ is injective by (b). It is surjective: $f_x(x^{-1}z)=x(x^{-1}z)=z$. The argument for $g_x$ is the same (with $g_x(zx^{-1})=z$). ∎

(b) (1 point) Explain why $(\mathbb Z,\cdot,1)$ and $(\mathbb Q,\cdot,0)$ are not groups ($\cdot$ is the usual multiplication; the third entry is the claimed identity).
answer: (a) closure, $1$, inverse $1/z$; (b) $2\in\mathbb Z$ has no integer inverse; in $(\mathbb Q,\cdot,0)$ $0\cdot x\ne x$.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
**(a)** If $z^m=w^m=1$ then $(zw)^m=1$, so $\mu_m$ is closed under multiplication. $1\in\mu_m$ is the identity. Each $z\in\mu_m$ is nonzero, and $(1/z)^m=1$, so $z^{-1}\in\mu_m$. Associativity and commutativity are inherited from $\mathbb C$. So $\mu_m$ is an abelian group.

*(Power Round, Problem 2.22)* A **group** is a nonempty set $G$ with an identity $e\in G$ and a binary operation $\cdot:G\times G\to G$ such that: (associativity) $x(yz)=(xy)z$; (identity) $ex=xe=x$; (inverse) for each $x$ there is $y$ with $xy=yx=e$ (written $x^{-1}$). It is **abelian** if also $xy=yx$. A nonempty subset $H$ of $G$ is a **subgroup** ($H\le G$) if $xy\in H$ and $x^{-1}\in H$ for all $x,y\in H$. For $g\in G$, the **left coset** is $gH=\{gh:h\in H\}$ and the right coset is $Hg=\{hg:h\in H\}$.

Let $H\le G$ be a subgroup and $g,g'\in G$.

(a) (1 point) Show that $gH$ (resp. $Hg$) is a subgroup of $G$ if and only if $g\in H$, in which case $gH=H$.

(b) (1 point) Show that $|gH|=|H|$ and $|Hg|=|H|$.

(c) (1 point) Show that the left cosets of $H$ partition $G$: either $gH=g'H$ or $gH\cap g'H=\varnothing$. Prove the same for right cosets.

(d) (1 point) (**Lagrange's theorem**) If $G$ is finite, show that the number of distinct left (resp. right) cosets of $H$ is $|G|/|H|$.
answer: Standard coset facts: $gH=H$ iff $g\in H$; $h\mapsto gh$ is a bijection; cosets partition $G$; hence $|G|=[G:H]\,|H|$.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
**(a)** If $gH$ is a subgroup it contains $e$, so $e=gh$ for some $h\in H$ and $g=h^{-1}\in H$. Conversely let $g\in H$. Then $gH\subseteq H$ by closure, and any $h\in H$ equals $g(g^{-1}h)\in gH$ as $g^{-1}h\in H$. So $gH=H$, a subgroup. The same works for $Hg$.

**(b)** $h\mapsto gh$ is a bijection $H\to gH$ (injective by cancellation, onto by definition). Likewise $h\mapsto hg$.

**(c)** Suppose $x\in gH\cap g'H$, $x=gh=g'h'$. Then $g=g'h'h^{-1}$, so $gH=g'(h'h^{-1}H)=g'H$ because $h'h^{-1}\in H$ and $kH=H$ for $k\in H$ by (a). So two left cosets are equal or disjoint, and every $g\in G$ lies in $gH$. Right cosets: $x=hg=h'g'$ gives $g=h^{-1}h'g'$ and $Hg=Hg'$.

**(d)** By (c) the distinct left cosets partition $G$ into pieces each of size $|H|$ by (b). So $|G|=(\#\text{cosets})\cdot|H|$. The same for right cosets. ∎

(a) (1 point) Show that $((\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z)^\times,\cdot,\bar1)$ is a group, where $(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z)^\times$ is the set of cosets $\bar k$ such that every integer in $k+m\mathbb Z$ is relatively prime to $m$, and $\bar k\cdot\bar l=\overline{kl}$.

solutions.body:

The **direct product** of groups $G_1,\dots,G_n$ is the group on $G_1\times\cdots\times G_n$ with componentwise multiplication. Let $m>1$ have prime factorization $m=p_1^{a_1}\cdots p_n^{a_n}$ with $a_i\ge1$ and put $q_i=p_i^{a_i}$. $\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z$ is the additive group of residues mod $m$, and $(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z)^\times$ the multiplicative group of residues coprime to $m$. (a) (2 points) $\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z\cong\mathbb Z/q_1\mathbb Z\times\cdots\times\mathbb Z/q_n\mathbb Z$ (Chinese Remainder Theorem).

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:

**(b)** The product $\psi(\bar k\bar l)=\psi(\bar k)\psi(\bar l)$ is componentwise multiplication as well ($kl\bmod q_i$). Now $\gcd(k,m)=1$ iff no $p_i$ divides $k$ iff $\gcd(k,q_i)=1$ for every $i$. It is onto: given $(c_1,\dots,c_n)$ with $\gcd(c_i,q_i)=1$, part (a) gives $k$ with $k\equiv c_i\pmod{q_i}$ for all $i$, and then $\gcd(k,q_i)=1$ for all $i$, so $\gcd(k,m)=1$. prompt:
*(Power Round, Problem 3.1)* A **group** $G$ has an associative operation, an identity $e$ and inverses. A subgroup $H\le G$ is a nonempty subset closed under products and inverses; the left cosets $gH$ partition $G$, all have size $|H|$, so (Lagrange) $|G|=[G:H]\,|H|$ when $G$ is finite. $H$ is **normal** ($H\trianglelefteq G$) if $gHg^{-1}=H$ for all $g$; then $G/H$, the set of cosets with $gH\cdot g'H=gg'H$, is a group.

A group $G$ **acts** on a set $S$ if there is a map $(g,s)\mapsto g\cdot s$ with $e\cdot s=s$ and $g\cdot(h\cdot s)=(gh)\cdot s$. The **orbit** of $s$ is $\mathrm{Orb}(s)=\{g\cdot s:g\in G\}$ and the **stabilizer** is $\mathrm{Stab}(s)=\{g\in G:g\cdot s=s\}$. $G$ acts on itself by **conjugation** $x\cdot g=xgx^{-1}$; the orbits are the **conjugacy classes**, and the stabilizer of $g$ is the **centralizer** $C_G(g)=\{x:xg=gx\}$.

Prove the **Orbit-Stabilizer Theorem**: for a finite group $G$ acting on a set $S$ and $s\in S$, $|\mathrm{Orb}(s)|\cdot|\mathrm{Stab}(s)|=|G|$.
answer: Cosets of $\mathrm{Stab}(s)$ correspond bijectively to points of $\mathrm{Orb}(s)$ via $g\,\mathrm{Stab}(s)\mapsto g\cdot s$; then apply Lagrange.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
Let $K=\mathrm{Stab}(s)$. It is a subgroup: $e\cdot s=s$; if $g\cdot s=s=h\cdot s$ then $(gh)\cdot s=g\cdot(h\cdot s)=s$ and $g^{-1}\cdot s=g^{-1}\cdot(g\cdot s)=(g^{-1}g)\cdot s=s$.

Define $f:G/K\to\mathrm{Orb}(s)$ by $f(gK)=g\cdot s$. For $g,g'\in G$:
$$g\cdot s=g'\cdot s\iff (g^{-1}g')\cdot s=s\iff g^{-1}g'\in K\iff gK=g'K.$$
The implication "$\Leftarrow$" shows $f$ is well defined and "$\Rightarrow$" shows it is injective. It is onto by definition of the orbit. Hence $|\mathrm{Orb}(s)|=[G:K]=|G|/|K|$ by Lagrange, i.e. $|\mathrm{Orb}(s)|\cdot|\mathrm{Stab}(s)|=|G|$. ∎

prompt:

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
Let $N\trianglelefteq S_n$. Then $N\cap A_n$ is normal in $A_n$, so by simplicity $N\cap A_n=A_n$ or $\{e\}$.

*Case $N\cap A_n=A_n$*, i.e. $A_n\subseteq N$. Then $|N|$ is a multiple of $|A_n|=n!/2$ (Lagrange) and divides $n!$, so $|N|=n!/2$ ($N=A_n$) or $n!$ ($N=S_n$).

*Case $N\cap A_n=\{e\}$.* The restriction of $\mathrm{sgn}$ to $N$ has kernel $N\cap A_n=\{e\}$, so it is injective and $|N|\le2$. Suppose $N=\{e,t\}$. For all $\tau\in S_n$, $\tau t\tau^{-1}\in N\setminus\{e\}$, so $\tau t=t\tau$: $t$ is central. But $t\ne e$ moves some $i$ to $j\ne i$; choose $k\notin\{i,j\}$ ($n\ge3$) and $\tau=(j\ k)$. Then $\tau t\tau^{-1}(i)=\tau(t(i))=\tau(j)=k\ne j=t(i)$, contradicting centrality. So $N=\{e\}$. ∎

By Problem 3.6, $\tau\sigma\tau^{-1}$ is obtained by replacing every entry $x$ in the cycles of $\sigma$ by $\tau(x)$. So $\tau\sigma\tau^{-1}=\sigma$ iff the cycles $(\tau(a_1)\cdots\tau(a_i))$, over all cycles $(a_1\cdots a_i)$ of $\sigma$, are exactly the cycles of $\sigma$, each as a cyclic sequence (the cycle decomposition is unique up to the order of cycles and cyclic rotation). Thus $\tau$ is in the centralizer iff it maps each cycle of $\sigma$ onto a cycle of $\sigma$ of the same length, preserving the cyclic order.

Choosing such a $\tau$ amounts to: for each length $i$, a bijection between the $a_i$ cycles of length $i$ and themselves ($a_i!$ choices), and for each cycle a rotation, i.e. which element of the target cycle receives $a_1$ ($i$ choices, so $i^{a_i}$ for all length-$i$ cycles). Different choices give different $\tau$, and every centralizing $\tau$ arises. Hence $|C_{S_n}(\sigma)|=\prod_ia_i!\,i^{a_i}$ and the formula follows. ∎

prompt:
*(Power Round, Problem 3.9)* $S_n$ is the group of permutations of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ (composition: the right factor acts first), $\mathrm{sgn}:S_n\to\{\pm1\}$ is the sign homomorphism ($+1$ on products of an even number of transpositions) and $A_n=\ker\mathrm{sgn}$.

A **group** $G$ has an associative operation, an identity $e$ and inverses. A subgroup $H\le G$ is a nonempty subset closed under products and inverses; the left cosets $gH$ partition $G$, all have size $|H|$, so (Lagrange) $|G|=[G:H]\,|H|$ when $G$ is finite. $H$ is **normal** ($H\trianglelefteq G$) if $gHg^{-1}=H$ for all $g$; then $G/H$, the set of cosets with $gH\cdot g'H=gg'H$, is a group.

Let $H\trianglelefteq G$. If a conjugacy class $K$ of $G$ is contained in $H$, then $K$ is a disjoint union of conjugacy classes of $H$ (two elements of $H$ are $H$-conjugate if $y=hxh^{-1}$ with $h\in H$); we say $K$ **splits** into $k$ conjugacy classes of $H$.

(a) (5 points) Let $G$ be finite and $H$ a normal subgroup. Show that if a conjugacy class $K$ of $G$ splits into $k$ conjugacy classes of $H$, then each of the $k$ classes has the same size.

(b) (3 points) Now let $G=S_n$ and $H=A_n$. Show that $k=1$ or $k=2$, and that $k=2$ iff no element of $K$ commutes with an odd permutation.
answer: (a) conjugation by $g\in G$ maps $H$-classes bijectively to $H$-classes; (b) compare $|C_{S_n}(x)|$ with $|C_{A_n}(x)|$ using orbit-stabilizer.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
**(a)** For $g\in G$ let $c_g(x)=gxg^{-1}$, a bijection of $K$ onto itself. For $x\in K$ the $H$-class of $x$ is $\{hxh^{-1}:h\in H\}$, and
$$c_g(hxh^{-1})=(ghg^{-1})\,c_g(x)\,(ghg^{-1})^{-1}.$$
As $h$ ranges over $H$, $ghg^{-1}$ ranges over all of $H$ (normality, and $c_g$ is a bijection on $H$). Hence $c_g$ maps the $H$-class of $x$ onto the $H$-class of $c_g(x)$, bijectively, so these two $H$-classes have equal size. Any two elements of $K$ are $G$-conjugate, so any two $H$-classes in $K$ have the same size.

**(b)** Fix $x\in K\subseteq A_n$. By Orbit-Stabilizer, $|K|=n!/|C_{S_n}(x)|$ and the $A_n$-class of $x$ has size $(n!/2)/|C_{A_n}(x)|$, where $C_{A_n}(x)=C_{S_n}(x)\cap A_n$.

- If $C_{S_n}(x)$ contains an odd permutation, then $\mathrm{sgn}$ restricted to $C_{S_n}(x)$ is onto $\{\pm1\}$ with kernel $C_{A_n}(x)$, so $|C_{A_n}(x)|=|C_{S_n}(x)|/2$ and the $A_n$-class of $x$ has size $|K|$: $K$ does not split ($k=1$).
- Otherwise $C_{S_n}(x)\subseteq A_n$, $C_{A_n}(x)=C_{S_n}(x)$, and the $A_n$-class of $x$ has size $|K|/2$. By (a) all $A_n$-classes in $K$ have this size, so $k=2$.

The condition does not depend on $x\in K$: $C(gxg^{-1})=gC(x)g^{-1}$ and conjugation preserves sign. So $k\in\{1,2\}$, and $k=2$ iff no element of $K$ commutes with an odd permutation. ∎

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
Write $g=c_1\cdots c_r$ as a product of disjoint cycles (including $1$-cycles) of lengths $\ell_1,\dots,\ell_r$.

**($\Rightarrow$)** Suppose the lengths are not all distinct and odd.
- If some $\ell_i$ is even, then $c_i$ commutes with $g$ (disjoint cycles commute), and $\mathrm{sgn}(c_i)=(-1)^{\ell_i-1}=-1$ (Problem 3.8): $g$ commutes with an odd permutation.
- If two cycles $(a_1\cdots a_\ell)$ and $(b_1\cdots b_\ell)$ have the same odd length $\ell$, let $\tau$ swap $a_j\leftrightarrow b_j$ for all $j$ ($\ell$ transpositions, $\ell$ odd, so $\tau$ is odd), fixing everything else. By Problem 3.6, $\tau g\tau^{-1}$ swaps the two cycles and fixes the others, so $\tau g\tau^{-1}=g$.

**($\Leftarrow$)** Suppose the lengths are distinct and odd and $\tau g=g\tau$. By the argument in Problem 3.7, $\tau$ maps each cycle of $g$ onto a cycle of the same length preserving cyclic order; the lengths are distinct, so $\tau$ maps each cycle $c_i$ onto itself, acting on its entries as a rotation, i.e. as a power $c_i^{r_i}$. Therefore $\tau=\prod c_i^{r_i}$ (the cycles are disjoint). Each $c_i$ has odd length, so is even (Problem 3.8), hence all $c_i^{r_i}$ and their product $\tau$ are even. So $g$ commutes with no odd permutation. ∎

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
**(a)** For $g,h\in G$, $gH\cdot hH=hH\cdot gH$ in the abelian group $G/H$, so $ghH=hgH$ and $(hg)^{-1}gh=g^{-1}h^{-1}gh\in H$. This is the commutator $[g^{-1},h^{-1}]$; as $g,h$ range over $G$ so do $g^{-1},h^{-1}$, so every commutator lies in $H$. Since $H$ is a subgroup, $G'\subseteq H$.

**(b)** Define $\psi:G^{ab}\to G/H$ by $\psi(gG')=gH$. It is well defined because $gG'=g'G'$ means $g^{-1}g'\in G'\subseteq H$, so $gH=g'H$; it is a homomorphism and onto. Its kernel is $N=\{gG':g\in H\}=H/G'$, a normal subgroup of $G^{ab}$. The map $G^{ab}/N\to G/H$, $aN\mapsto\psi(a)$, is well defined (since $aN=a'N$ means $a^{-1}a'\in N=\ker\psi$), a homomorphism, injective (if $\psi(a)=e$ then $a\in N$) and surjective. So $G/H\cong G^{ab}/(H/G')$, a quotient of $G^{ab}$. ∎

prompt: *(Power Round, Problem 3.14)* For $g,h$ in a group $G$ let $[g,h]=ghg^{-1}h^{-1}$; $G'$ is the (normal) subgroup generated by all commutators, $G^{ab}=G/G'$, and $p:G\to G^{ab}$, $g\mapsto gG'$ is the projection. solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
Since $H$ is abelian, $\varphi([g,k])=[\varphi(g),\varphi(k)]=e$, so every commutator lies in $\ker\varphi$. As $\ker\varphi$ is a subgroup, $G'\subseteq\ker\varphi$.

*Existence.* Define $h(gG')=\varphi(g)$. It is well defined: if $gG'=g'G'$ then $g^{-1}g'\in G'\subseteq\ker\varphi$, so $\varphi(g)=\varphi(g')$. It is a homomorphism: $h(gG'\cdot g'G')=h(gg'G')=\varphi(gg')=\varphi(g)\varphi(g')$. And $h(p(g))=\varphi(g)$.

*Uniqueness.* If $h'\circ p=\varphi=h\circ p$, then $h'(gG')=h(gG')$ for every $g$, and every element of $G^{ab}$ has the form $gG'=p(g)$. So $h'=h$. ∎

solutions.title: Solution
solutions.body:
**(a)** For $g\in G$, the map $s\mapsto g\cdot s$ is a bijection of $S$ (inverse $s\mapsto g^{-1}\cdot s$), so define $\pi_g\in S_n$ by $g\cdot s_j=s_{\pi_g(j)}$. **(b)** $\phi(g)$ sends $e_j\mapsto e_{\pi_g(j)}$, which is exactly $\psi(\pi_g)$. So every element of $\mathrm{im}(\phi)$ lies in $\mathrm{im}(\psi)$. $\mathrm{im}(\phi)$ is a subgroup of $GL_n(\mathbb C)$ (image of a homomorphism, Problem 2.24), hence a subgroup of $\mathrm{im}(\psi)$.

**(c)** $f(g)=\pi_g$ is well defined since $\phi(g)\in\mathrm{im}\psi$. Then $\psi(f(g)f(h))=\psi(f(g))\psi(f(h))=\phi(g)\phi(h)=\phi(gh)=\psi(f(gh))$, and injectivity of $\psi$ gives $f(gh)=f(g)f(h)$. ∎

solutions.title: Verification
solutions.body:

**Maschke's Theorem.** If $(U,\phi_U)$ is a subrepresentation of $(V,\phi)$, then there is a subrepresentation $W$ with $V=U\oplus W$. Prove it as follows.

(a) (1 point) Show that there is a (not necessarily $G$-stable) subspace $W_0$ with $V=U\oplus W_0$.

(b) (2 points) Define $\pi_0:V\to U$ by $\pi_0(u+w)=u$ ($u\in U$, $w\in W_0$). For $g\in G$ define $g\pi_0g^{-1}:V\to U$ by $v\mapsto\phi_U(g)\pi_0(\phi(g^{-1})v)$. Verify that $g\pi_0g^{-1}(u)=u$ for all $u\in U$.

(c) (4 points) Let $\pi(v)=\frac1{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}g\pi_0g^{-1}(v)$. Prove: (i) $\pi$ is linear; (ii) $\pi(u)=u$ for $u\in U$; (iii) $\pi(\pi(v))=\pi(v)$; (iv) $\pi$ is $G$-linear.

(d) (3 points) Let $W=\ker\pi$. Show that $W$ is $G$-stable and $V=U\oplus W$.
answer: Average a projection onto $U$ over the group to get a $G$-linear projection; its kernel is a $G$-stable complement.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
**(a)** If $U=0$ take $W_0=V$; if $U=V$ take $W_0=0$; otherwise Problem 1.5(b) gives a complement.

**(b)** For $u\in U$, $\phi(g^{-1})u\in U$ (as $U$ is stable), so $\pi_0(\phi(g^{-1})u)=\phi(g^{-1})u$ and $g\pi_0g^{-1}(u)=\phi(g)\phi(g^{-1})u=u$.

**(c)** (i) Each $g\pi_0g^{-1}$ is a composition of linear maps; a linear combination is linear. (ii) For $u\in U$, $\pi(u)=\frac1{|G|}\sum_g u=u$ by (b). (iii) Every $g\pi_0g^{-1}$ maps into $U$, so $\pi(v)\in U$ and by (ii) $\pi(\pi(v))=\pi(v)$. (iv) For $h\in G$,
$$\pi(\phi(h)v)=\frac1{|G|}\sum_g\phi(g)\pi_0\phi(g^{-1}h)v=\frac1{|G|}\sum_k\phi(hk)\pi_0\phi(k^{-1})v=\phi(h)\pi(v),$$
substituting $g=hk$ (as $g$ runs over $G$ so does $k=h^{-1}g$). So $\pi\phi(h)=\phi(h)\pi$ (viewing $\pi$ as a map $V\to U\subseteq V$).

**(d)** $W=\ker\pi$ is a subrepresentation by Problem 4.7(a). For $v\in V$, $v=\pi(v)+(v-\pi(v))$ with $\pi(v)\in U$ and $\pi(v-\pi(v))=\pi(v)-\pi(\pi(v))=0$, so $v-\pi(v)\in W$: $V=U+W$. If $u\in U\cap W$ then $u=\pi(u)=0$. So $V=U\oplus W$. ∎

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
Class functions are closed under addition and scalar multiples, so $\mathbb C_{\rm class}(G)$ is a vector space. For $\chi,\chi',\psi,\psi'$ and $c\in\mathbb C$:
- Additivity: $\langle\chi+\chi',\psi\rangle=\frac1{|G|}\sum(\chi+\chi')\overline\psi=\langle\chi,\psi\rangle+\langle\chi',\psi\rangle$, and likewise in the second slot since $\overline{\psi+\psi'}=\bar\psi+\bar\psi'$.
- Homogeneity: $\langle c\chi,\psi\rangle=c\langle\chi,\psi\rangle$ and $\langle\chi,c\psi\rangle=\bar c\langle\chi,\psi\rangle$.
- Conjugate symmetry: $\overline{\langle\psi,\chi\rangle}=\frac1{|G|}\sum\overline{\psi(g)}\chi(g)=\langle\chi,\psi\rangle$.
- Positivity/definiteness: $\langle\chi,\chi\rangle=\frac1{|G|}\sum|\chi(g)|^2\ge0$, with equality iff $\chi(g)=0$ for every $g$, i.e. $\chi=0$. ∎

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
**Trace of $f\mapsto BfA$.** Fix bases of $V$ ($n$ elements) and $W$ ($m$ elements); identify $f$ with an $m\times n$ matrix, with basis $E_{ij}$ (a $1$ in row $i$, column $j$). With $A=\phi_1(g)$ and $B=\phi_2(g^{-1})$ this gives $\chi(g)=\chi_V(g)\chi_W(g^{-1})$.

**Dimension.** By Problem 5.5(b) applied to the representation $g\mapsto(f\mapsto g\cdot f)$ of Problem 4.5, whose character is $g\mapsto\chi_V(g^{-1})\chi_W(g)$ (same computation with $A=\phi_1(g)^{-1}$, $B=\phi_2(g)$), and by $\mathrm{Hom}(V,W)^G=\mathrm{Hom}_G(V,W)$,
$$\dim\mathrm{Hom}_G(V,W)=\frac1{|G|}\sum_g\chi_V(g^{-1})\chi_W(g)=\frac1{|G|}\sum_g\chi_V(g)\chi_W(g^{-1}),$$
the last step by reindexing $g\mapsto g^{-1}$. ∎

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
Let $m$ be the order of $g$. Then $\phi(g)^m=\phi(g^m)=I$, so the minimal polynomial of $\phi(g)$ divides $x^m-1$, which has $m$ distinct roots (the $m$th roots of unity). Hence $\phi(g)$ is diagonalizable, and in an eigenbasis its diagonal entries $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_d$ are $m$th roots of unity. Then $\chi(g)=\sum\lambda_i$ is a sum of roots of unity.

The matrix of $\phi(g^{-1})=\phi(g)^{-1}$ in the same basis is $\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_i^{-1})$, and $\lambda_i^{-1}=\overline{\lambda_i}$ since $|\lambda_i|=1$. So $\chi(g^{-1})=\sum\overline{\lambda_i}=\overline{\chi(g)}$. ∎

(a) (2 points) Prove that for any decomposition $V=V_1\oplus\cdots\oplus V_s$ into irreducible subrepresentations, the number of $V_j$ equivalent to $U_i$ equals $\langle\chi,\chi_i\rangle$. Deduce $\chi=\sum_i\langle\chi,\chi_i\rangle\chi_i$.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:

So $V\cong U_1^{\oplus n_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus U_r^{\oplus n_r}\cong W$: choose equivalences between matching summands and assemble them into one invertible $G$-linear map $V\to W$. ∎

**Theorem 5.4.** The irreducible characters $\chi_1,\dots,\chi_r$ of $G$ form an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb C_{\rm class}(G)$; in particular the number of inequivalent irreducible representations equals the number of conjugacy classes. (Recall $\dim\mathbb C_{\rm class}(G)$ is the number of conjugacy classes.)

Prove Theorem 5.4. Hint: for a class function $\alpha$ and a representation $(V,\phi)$ consider $\rho_{\alpha,V}=\sum_g\alpha(g)\phi(g)$ and check it is $G$-linear.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
The $\chi_i$ are class functions (Problem 5.3) and orthonormal (First Orthogonality), hence linearly independent. It remains to show they span. Let $\alpha\in\mathbb C_{\rm class}(G)$ with $\langle\alpha,\chi_i\rangle=0$ for all $i$; we show $\alpha=0$ (then the orthogonal complement of the span is $0$, so the span is everything).

For a representation $(V,\phi)$ put $\rho_V=\sum_g\overline{\alpha(g)}\phi(g)$. For $h\in G$, using that $\alpha$ is a class function and reindexing $g'=hgh^{-1}$,
$$\phi(h)\rho_V\phi(h)^{-1}=\sum_g\overline{\alpha(g)}\phi(hgh^{-1})=\sum_{g'}\overline{\alpha(g')}\phi(g')=\rho_V,$$
so $\rho_V$ is $G$-linear.

*Irreducible $V$ with character $\chi_i$:* by Schur, $\rho_V=\lambda I$, and taking traces, $\lambda\dim V=\sum_g\overline{\alpha(g)}\chi_i(g)=\overline{\sum_g\alpha(g)\overline{\chi_i(g)}}=|G|\overline{\langle\alpha,\chi_i\rangle}=0$. So $\rho_V=0$.

*Any $V$:* decompose $V$ into irreducible subrepresentations (Maschke). $\rho_V$ preserves each summand and acts on it as the corresponding $\rho$, which is $0$. So $\rho_V=0$.

Take $V=\mathbb C[G]$, the regular representation: $0=\rho_V(e)=\sum_g\overline{\alpha(g)}\,g$, where $e$ is the identity element (a basis vector). The group elements are a basis, so $\alpha(g)=0$ for all $g$. Hence $\alpha=0$ and the $\chi_i$ are an orthonormal basis of $\mathbb C_{\rm class}(G)$; their number is $\dim\mathbb C_{\rm class}(G)$, the number of conjugacy classes. ∎

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
Let $\chi$ be the character of $V$, $d=\dim V$, $Z=Z(G)$. For $z\in Z$, $\phi(z)$ commutes with every $\phi(g)$, so it is $G$-linear, and by Schur's Lemma $\phi(z)=\omega I$. As $z$ has finite order $m$, $\omega^m=1$, so $|\omega|=1$ and $|\chi(z)|=|\omega d|=d$.

(a) (3 points) Let a finite group $G$ act on a finite set $S$ and $V=\mathbb C[S]$ the corresponding representation. Prove that $\dim V^G$ is the number of orbits of $G$ on $S$.

(b) (5 points) Let $n\ge2$ and let $W=\mathbb C[\{1,\dots,n\}]$ be the permutation representation of $S_n$. Prove $W=U\oplus V$ as representations of $S_n$, with $U$ equivalent to the trivial representation and $V$ an irreducible subrepresentation of dimension $n-1$.
answer: (a) $G$-fixed vectors are constant on orbits; (b) $U$ is spanned by $\sum e_i$, $V$ is the sum-zero vectors; irreducibility from $\langle\chi_V,\chi_V\rangle=1$ via Burnside counting.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
**(a)** A vector $v=\sum_sc_ss$ satisfies $g\cdot v=\sum c_s(g\cdot s)=\sum_sc_{g^{-1}s}s$. So $v\in V^G$ iff $c_{g^{-1}s}=c_s$ for all $g,s$, i.e. $c$ is constant on each orbit. Thus $V^G$ has basis the orbit sums $\sum_{s\in O}s$, one per orbit, and $\dim V^G=\#\text{orbits}$.

**(b)** Let $U=\mathbb C(e_1+\cdots+e_n)$: each $\sigma$ fixes it, so it is a subrepresentation equivalent to the trivial one. Let $V=\{\sum c_ie_i:\sum c_i=0\}=\ker$ of the $S_n$-invariant linear functional $\sum c_i$; it is $G$-stable with $\dim V=n-1$. Every $w\in W$ is $w=\frac{\sum c_i}{n}(e_1+\cdots+e_n)+\big(w-\frac{\sum c_i}{n}(e_1+\cdots+e_n)\big)$ with the second part in $V$, and $U\cap V=0$ (since $n\ne0$). So $W=U\oplus V$.

*Irreducibility.* Let $\chi_W(\sigma)=\mathrm{fix}(\sigma)$ (Example 5.4) and $\chi_V=\chi_W-1$. Burnside count: $\sum_\sigma\mathrm{fix}(\sigma)=\sum_i|\mathrm{Stab}(i)|=\sum_i\frac{|G|}{|\mathrm{Orb}(i)|}=|G|\cdot\#\text{orbits}$ (orbit-stabilizer; the same for any action). Applying it to $S_n$ on $\{1,\dots,n\}$ (one orbit) gives $\langle\chi_W,1\rangle=1$. Applying it to $S_n$ on pairs $(i,j)$, where $\mathrm{fix}(\sigma)^2$ counts the fixed pairs, $\langle\chi_W,\chi_W\rangle=\frac1{n!}\sum\mathrm{fix}(\sigma)^2=\#\text{orbits on pairs}=2$ (the diagonal pairs and the pairs with $i\ne j$; $S_n$ is transitive on ordered pairs of distinct elements). Therefore
$$\langle\chi_V,\chi_V\rangle=\langle\chi_W,\chi_W\rangle-2\langle\chi_W,1\rangle+\langle1,1\rangle=2-2+1=1.$$
Writing $\chi_V=\sum a_i\chi_i$ in irreducibles gives $\sum a_i^2=1$, so $V$ is irreducible. ∎

Prove the **Second Orthogonality Relation**: for $x,y\in G$,
$$\sum_{i=1}^r\chi_i(x)\overline{\chi_i(y)}=\begin{cases}0&x,y\text{ not conjugate},\\ |C_G(x)|&x,y\text{ conjugate},\end{cases}$$
where $C_G(x)$ is the centralizer of $x$.
answer: Rewrite First Orthogonality as $XDX^\dagger=I$ with $D=\mathrm{diag}(1/|C_G(g_j)|)$, then invert.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
Let $K_j$ be the conjugacy class of $g_j$; $|K_j|=|G|/|C_G(g_j)|$ by orbit-stabilizer. Class functions are constant on $K_j$, so the First Orthogonality Relation reads
$$\delta_{ik}=\frac1{|G|}\sum_j|K_j|\chi_i(g_j)\overline{\chi_k(g_j)}=\sum_j\chi_i(g_j)\frac1{|C_G(g_j)|}\overline{\chi_k(g_j)},$$
i.e. $XDX^\dagger=I$ with $D=\mathrm{diag}(1/|C_G(g_j)|)$ and $X^\dagger$ the conjugate transpose. All matrices are $r\times r$, so $X$ is invertible with $X^{-1}=DX^\dagger$; hence also $DX^\dagger X=I$, i.e. $X^\dagger X=D^{-1}$:
$$\sum_i\overline{\chi_i(g_j)}\chi_i(g_l)=\delta_{jl}|C_G(g_j)|.$$
Taking complex conjugates (the right side is real) gives $\sum_i\chi_i(g_j)\overline{\chi_i(g_l)}=\delta_{jl}|C_G(g_j)|$. For arbitrary $x,y$, each $\chi_i$ takes the same value on conjugate elements, so replace $x,y$ by the representatives of their classes: the sum is $0$ if the classes differ, and $|C_G(x)|$ if they coincide (centralizers of conjugate elements have equal size). ∎

prompt:
*(Power Round, Problem 5.14)* The **character table** of a finite group $G$ is the square matrix $(\chi_i(g_j))$ where $\chi_1,\dots,\chi_r$ are the distinct irreducible (complex) characters and $g_1,\dots,g_r$ represent the $r$ conjugacy classes (the table is labelled with the class sizes). Write down the character tables of the following groups:

(a) (2 points) $Q_8$ (quaternion group of order 8).

(b) (3 points) $D_5$ (dihedral group of order 10).

(c) (5 points) $S_4$ and $A_4$.

(d) (12 points) $A_5$.

No explanations are needed for (a), (b), (c). A proof is required for (d).

solutions.title: Proof for (d): $A_5$
solutions.body:
**Classes.** The classes of $S_5$ inside $A_5$ are the cycle types $1^5$, $2^21$, $3\,1^2$, $5$ with sizes $1,15,20,24$. By Problems 3.9 and 3.10 only the type with distinct odd parts, $(5)$, splits in $A_5$, into two classes of size $12$. So $A_5$ has $r=5$ classes: $1$ (size 1), $(12)(34)$ (15), $(123)$ (20), and two classes of $5$-cycles $5A,5B$ (12 each), and hence $5$ irreducible characters, with $\sum(\dim\chi_i)^2=60$.

**The trivial character** $\chi_1$.

**A 4-dimensional character.** $A_5$ acts on $\{1,\dots,5\}$; the permutation character is $\mathrm{fix}$, with values $5,1,2,0,0$ on the five classes. $\langle\mathrm{fix},1\rangle=1$ (one orbit, Problem 5.12(a)) and $\langle\mathrm{fix},\mathrm{fix}\rangle=\frac{25+15\cdot1+20\cdot4}{60}=2$. Hence $\mathrm{fix}=1+\chi_4$ with $\chi_4$ irreducible of degree 4 and values $(4,0,1,-1,-1)$.

**A 5-dimensional character.** $A_5$ is simple, so its Sylow 5-subgroups are not normal and the number of them is $\equiv1\pmod5$ and divides $12$: it is $6$. Let $A_5$ act on these 6 subgroups by conjugation, with permutation character $\psi$. Let $P$ be a Sylow 5-subgroup; its normalizer has order $60/6=10$, so it contains $P$ and $5$ involutions (an element of order $10$ does not exist in $A_5$), and its elements of order $5$ are those of $P$.
- A $5$-element $x$ fixes $Q$ iff $x\in N(Q)$ iff $x\in Q$: exactly one fixed point. So $\psi=1$ on $5A,5B$.
- An element of order 3 lies in no $N(Q)$ (order 10): $\psi=0$.
- Counting pairs (involution, Sylow subgroup whose normalizer contains it): $6\cdot5=30$ pairs and $15$ involutions, all conjugate, so each fixes $2$ points: $\psi=2$.

So $\psi=(6,2,0,1,1)$ and $\langle\psi,\psi\rangle=\frac{36+15\cdot4+0+12+12}{60}=2$, $\langle\psi,1\rangle=1$. Hence $\psi=1+\chi_5$ with $\chi_5$ irreducible, values $(5,1,-1,0,0)$.

**The two remaining characters.** $60-1-16-25=18$, so the other two irreducible degrees satisfy $a^2+b^2=18$, i.e. $a=b=3$. Let $\chi$ be either of them with values $(3,a_2,a_3,c,\tilde c)$. Orthogonality to $1,\chi_4,\chi_5$ (all real) gives, with class sizes $1,15,20,12,12$:
$$3+15a_2+20a_3+12(c+\tilde c)=0,\quad 12+20a_3-12(c+\tilde c)=0,\quad 15+15a_2-20a_3=0.$$
Adding the first two and using the third: $15+15a_2+40a_3=0$ and $15+15a_2=20a_3$, so $60a_3=0$, $a_3=0$, then $a_2=-1$ and $c+\tilde c=1$.

Moreover a $5$-cycle $g=(1\,2\,3\,4\,5)$ is conjugate to $g^{-1}$ by the even permutation $(1\,5)(2\,4)$, so $\chi(g)=\chi(g^{-1})=\overline{\chi(g)}$ is real (Problem 5.7), and the same for the other class. Then $\langle\chi,\chi\rangle=1$ gives $\frac{9+15+12(c^2+\tilde c^2)}{60}=1$, so $c^2+\tilde c^2=3$. With $c+\tilde c=1$ this gives $c\tilde c=-1$, so $\{c,\tilde c\}=\{\frac{1+\sqrt5}2,\frac{1-\sqrt5}2\}$. The two characters agree on the first three classes and are distinct, so they take the two possible orders.

**Result.** With $\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2$, $\bar\varphi=\frac{1-\sqrt5}2=1-\varphi$:

| class | $1$ | $(12)(34)$ | $(123)$ | $5A$ | $5B$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| size | 1 | 15 | 20 | 12 | 12 |
| $\chi_1$ | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| $\chi_2$ | 3 | $-1$ | 0 | $\varphi$ | $\bar\varphi$ |
| $\chi_3$ | 3 | $-1$ | 0 | $\bar\varphi$ | $\varphi$ |
| $\chi_4$ | 4 | 0 | 1 | $-1$ | $-1$ |
| $\chi_5$ | 5 | 1 | $-1$ | 0 | 0 |

Check: $1+9+9+16+25=60$. ∎

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
($\Leftarrow$) If $g^{-1}=xgx^{-1}$ then for every character $\chi_i(g^{-1})=\chi_i(g)$, while $\chi_i(g^{-1})=\overline{\chi_i(g)}$. So $\chi_i(g)=\overline{\chi_i(g)}$ is real.

($\Rightarrow$) Suppose every $\chi_i(g)$ is real. Then $\overline{\chi_i(g^{-1})}=\chi_i(g)$, so
$$\sum_i\chi_i(g)\overline{\chi_i(g^{-1})}=\sum_i\chi_i(g)^2=\sum_i|\chi_i(g)|^2=\sum_i\chi_i(g)\overline{\chi_i(g)}=|C_G(g)|\ne0,$$
using the Second Orthogonality Relation for $x=y=g$. By the same relation with $x=g$, $y=g^{-1}$, the left-hand side is $0$ unless $g$ and $g^{-1}$ are conjugate. Hence they are conjugate. ∎

solutions.body: By Problem 3.10, $g$ commutes with some odd permutation, so by Problem 3.9(b) the $S_n$-conjugacy class $K$ of $g$ does not split: it is a single $A_n$-class. Now $g^{-1}$ has the same cycle type as $g$, so $g^{-1}\in K$, i.e. $g^{-1}$ is conjugate to $g$ in $A_n$. ∎

Let $g\in A_n$ have cycle type consisting of $k$ distinct odd integers (cycle lengths $\ell_1,\dots,\ell_k$, with $\sum\ell_i=n$, counting a fixed point as a cycle of length 1). Show that $g$ and $g^{-1}$ are conjugate in $A_n$ if and only if $n\equiv k\pmod 4$.
answer: Every conjugator $g\to g^{-1}$ in $S_n$ has the same parity (centralizer is in $A_n$); the explicit one reversing each cycle has sign $(-1)^{(n-k)/2}$.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
By Problem 3.10 the centralizer $C_{S_n}(g)$ contains no odd permutation. If $\tau_0g\tau_0^{-1}=g^{-1}$, all permutations $\tau$ with $\tau g\tau^{-1}=g^{-1}$ are exactly $\tau_0c$ with $c\in C_{S_n}(g)\subseteq A_n$, so they all have the parity of $\tau_0$. Therefore $g$ and $g^{-1}$ are conjugate in $A_n$ iff $\tau_0$ is even.

Construct $\tau_0$: for a cycle $(a_1\,a_2\,\cdots\,a_\ell)$ of $g$ ($\ell$ odd) let $\tau$ send $a_j\mapsto a_{2-j}$ (indices mod $\ell$). By Problem 3.6, $\tau(a_1\cdots a_\ell)\tau^{-1}=(a_1\,a_\ell\,a_{\ell-1}\cdots a_2)$, the inverse cycle. $\tau$ fixes $a_1$ and swaps $a_j\leftrightarrow a_{2-j}$ for the other $\ell-1$ elements; since $\ell$ is odd, $j\equiv2-j$ forces $j\equiv1$, so these form $(\ell-1)/2$ transpositions. Let $\tau_0$ be the product of these maps over all cycles (disjoint supports). Then $\tau_0g\tau_0^{-1}=g^{-1}$ and
$$\mathrm{sgn}(\tau_0)=(-1)^{\sum_i(\ell_i-1)/2}=(-1)^{(n-k)/2}.$$
Since each $\ell_i$ is odd, $n\equiv k\pmod2$, so $(n-k)/2$ is an integer, and $\tau_0$ is even iff $(n-k)/2$ is even iff $n\equiv k\pmod4$. ∎

You may use Problems 6.1, 6.3 and 6.4 (for $g\in A_n$ with $k$ distinct odd cycle lengths, $g$ is conjugate to $g^{-1}$ in $A_n$ iff $n\equiv k\pmod4$). Let $n>1$. Show that $A_n$ has a real character table (all entries real) if and only if $n=2,5,6,10,14$.
answer: Real iff $n\equiv k\pmod 4$ for every $k$ with a partition of $n$ into $k$ distinct odd parts; such partitions exist iff $k^2\le n$ and $k\equiv n\pmod2$.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
By Problem 6.1 the table is real iff every $g\in A_n$ is conjugate in $A_n$ to $g^{-1}$. By Problem 6.3 only elements with $k$ distinct odd cycle lengths matter, and by 6.4 the condition is $n\equiv k\pmod4$ for every $k$ for which such an element exists, i.e. for which $n$ is a sum of $k$ distinct odd positive integers.

*Which $k$ occur.* The smallest sum of $k$ distinct odd numbers is $1+3+\cdots+(2k-1)=k^2$, and a sum of $k$ odd numbers has the parity of $k$. Conversely if $n\ge k^2$ and $n\equiv k\pmod2$, then $1,3,\dots,2k-3,\ n-(k-1)^2$ works: the last part is odd and $\ge2k-1$. So such $k$ exist exactly when $k\ge1$, $k^2\le n$, $k\equiv n\pmod2$.

*$n$ odd.* $k=1$ always occurs (the $n$-cycle), forcing $n\equiv1\pmod4$. If $n\ge9$, $k=3$ also occurs, forcing $n\equiv3\pmod 4$: contradiction. So $n\le8$, $n\equiv1\pmod 4$, $n>1$: $n=5$. (For $n=5$ only $k=1$ occurs, and $5\equiv1$.) The odd $n\equiv3\pmod4$ fail at $k=1$.

*$n$ even.* $n=2$: no $k$ (as $k=2$ needs $n\ge4$), so the condition is vacuous: $A_2$ is trivial and its table is real. For $n\ge4$, $k=2$ occurs (e.g. $1+(n-1)$), forcing $n\equiv2\pmod4$. If $n\ge16$, $k=4$ occurs, forcing $n\equiv0\pmod 4$: contradiction. So $n\equiv2\pmod4$ and $n<16$: $n=6,10,14$ (and $n=2$). For these, the only $k$ with $k^2\le n$, $k$ even is $k=2$ (as $16>14$), and $n\equiv2$ ✓.

Hence $A_n$ has a real character table iff $n\in\{2,5,6,10,14\}$. ∎

prompt:
*(Power Round, Problem 6.6)* Throughout, $G$ is a finite group, $\chi_1,\dots,\chi_r$ are its distinct irreducible complex characters (so $r$ is the number of conjugacy classes) and $g_1,\dots,g_r$ represent the conjugacy classes. You may use: the First and Second Orthogonality Relations ($\sum_i\chi_i(x)\overline{\chi_i(y)}=|C_G(x)|$ if $x,y$ are conjugate and $0$ otherwise); $\chi(g^{-1})=\overline{\chi(g)}$ for every character; characters are constant on conjugacy classes.

Call a conjugacy class $C$ **self-inverse** if $C^{-1}=\{x^{-1}:x\in C\}=C$. Show that for any finite group $G$, the number of real-valued irreducible characters of $G$ equals the number of self-inverse conjugacy classes of $G$.
answer: Complex conjugation permutes the irreducible characters, inversion permutes the classes, and the invertible character table intertwines the two permutation matrices, so they have equal traces.

solutions.title: Proof
solutions.body:
**Conjugate characters are irreducible.** If $\phi:G\to GL_d(\mathbb C)$ is a matrix representation, then $\bar\phi$ (entrywise complex conjugate) is also one, with character $\overline\chi$. If $\chi$ is irreducible then $\langle\bar\chi,\bar\chi\rangle=\overline{\langle\chi,\chi\rangle}=1$, and a character $\sum a_i\chi_i$ with $\sum a_i^2=1$ is irreducible. So there is a permutation $\sigma$ of $\{1,\dots,r\}$ with $\overline{\chi_i}=\chi_{\sigma(i)}$. The fixed points of $\sigma$ are exactly the real-valued irreducible characters.

**Inversion permutes classes.** $x\mapsto x^{-1}$ maps conjugacy classes onto conjugacy classes ($(yxy^{-1})^{-1}=yx^{-1}y^{-1}$), so there is a permutation $\tau$ with $g_j^{-1}\in\mathrm{class}(g_{\tau(j)})$. Its fixed points are exactly the self-inverse classes.

**Relation.** Let $X=(\chi_i(g_j))$ be the character table, invertible (Second Orthogonality, or Theorem 5.4). By $\chi_i(g^{-1})=\overline{\chi_i(g)}$,
$$X_{i,\tau(j)}=\chi_i(g_{\tau(j)})=\chi_i(g_j^{-1})=\overline{\chi_i(g_j)}=\chi_{\sigma(i)}(g_j)=X_{\sigma(i),j}.$$
Let $Q$ be the permutation matrix with $Q_{lj}=1$ iff $l=\tau(j)$ and $R$ the one with $R_{il}=1$ iff $l=\sigma(i)$. Then $(XQ)_{ij}=X_{i,\tau(j)}$ and $(RX)_{ij}=X_{\sigma(i),j}$, so $XQ=RX$, i.e. $R=XQX^{-1}$. Similar matrices have equal traces, and the trace of a permutation matrix is the number of fixed points of the permutation. So $\#\mathrm{Fix}(\sigma)=\#\mathrm{Fix}(\tau)$: the number of real irreducible characters equals the number of self-inverse conjugacy classes. ∎
